question: Y127
answer:
MEMORANDUM — SECTION 378, COMPANIES ACT 2006: DONATION CEILING AND MEASURING PERIOD

Prepared for: instructing attorney (review draft — not legal advice)
Jurisdiction: England and Wales, and (the section being expressed to extend to the United Kingdom) Scotland and Northern Ireland — Companies Act 2006 (c. 46), s. 378, extent marker "U.K."
Question: In the text of s. 378 stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026, what donation ceiling and measuring period does the section state?

1. SHORT ANSWER

1.1 Ceiling: £5,000.
1.2 Measuring period: the period of 12 months ending with the date on which the donation in question is made — i.e. a rolling, backward-looking 12-month window recalculated at the date of each donation, not a financial year, calendar year or fixed authorisation period.
1.3 Nature of the figure: £5,000 is a threshold, not a per-donation cap and not a per-recipient allowance. Authorisation under Part 14 is dispensed with only "to the extent that" the aggregate of the donation plus other relevant donations does not exceed £5,000; any excess above £5,000 requires authorisation (Companies Act 2006, s. 378(1)).

2. PRIMARY SOURCE CITED IN FULL

2.1 Companies Act 2006 (c. 46), Part 14 (Control of political donations and expenditure), section 378, headed "Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period", as revised and stated on legislation.gov.uk to be "up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026" (page fetched 23 November 2026), https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378.
2.2 Same provision as originally enacted: Companies Act 2006 (c. 46), s. 378, King's Printer copy of the Act as enacted (8 November 2006), https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/pdfs/ukpga_20060046_en_001.pdf and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/part/14/enacted.
2.3 Version snapshots checked: s. 378 as at 21 July 2025 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2025-07-21) and as at 5 June 2025 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378/2025-06-05).
2.4 Explanatory Notes to the Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), notes on Part 14, note on section 378 (the note beginning "section 376 restates the exemption in section 347B of the 1985 Act …"). Paragraph number not captured on the retrieved page and should be verified before citation in a filed document.
2.5 Commencement: Companies Act 2006 (Commencement No. 3, Consequential Amendments, Transitional Provisions and Savings) Order 2007 (S.I. 2007/2194), arts. 2(2), 3(1), 5(1)(i) (with saving in art. 12 and transitional provisions and savings in Sch. 3) — s. 378 wholly in force 1 October 2008; in force for certain purposes 1 October 2007 (E.W.S.) and 1 November 2007 (N.I.).
2.6 Modification: The Unregistered Companies Regulations 2009 (S.I. 2009/2436), regs. 3–5 and Sch. 1 para. 9 (with transitional provisions and savings in regs. 7, 9 and Sch. 2), applying ss. 362–379 with modifications from 1 October 2009.

3. THE TEXT OF SECTION 378 (reproduced verbatim)

"378 Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month period

(1) Authorisation under this Part is not needed for a donation except to the extent that the total amount of—
(a) that donation, and
(b) other relevant donations made in the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made,
exceeds £5,000.

(2) In this section—
"donation" means a donation to a political party or other political organisation or to an independent election candidate; and
"other relevant donations" means—
(a) in relation to a donation made by a company that is not a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company or by any of its subsidiaries;
(b) in relation to a donation made by a company that is a subsidiary, any other donations made by that company, by any holding company of that company or by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.

(3) If or to the extent that a donation is exempt by virtue of this section from the requirement of authorisation under this Part, it shall be disregarded in determining what donations are authorised by any resolution passed for the purposes of this Part."

4. ANALYSIS

4.1 The ceiling. The only monetary figure in the section is £5,000, appearing in the section heading ("more than £5,000 in any twelve month period") and in s. 378(1) ("exceeds £5,000"). There is no second figure, no per-recipient figure and no uprating mechanism in the section itself.

4.2 The measuring period. Section 378(1)(b) fixes it as "the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made". Three consequences follow from the words used:
(a) it looks backwards from the date of the donation under consideration, so the window moves with each donation and is not a fixed annual allowance;
(b) it is a single aggregate window for all relevant donations — donations to a political party, to another political organisation and to an independent election candidate all count against the same £5,000 (s. 378(1)(b) read with the definition of "donation" in s. 378(2));
(c) it is not the four-year period in s. 368 (period for which an authorising resolution has effect). The two periods operate differently and must not be conflated: s. 368 governs the life of a shareholder resolution; s. 378(1)(b) governs the calculation of the exemption.

4.3 Whose donations count. "Other relevant donations" is defined by reference to the company's group position (s. 378(2)):
(a) for a company that is not a subsidiary: donations by that company and by any of its subsidiaries;
(b) for a company that is a subsidiary: donations by that company, by any holding company of that company, and by any other subsidiary of any such holding company.
The £5,000 is therefore a group-aggregated threshold, not a company-by-company allowance. The Explanatory Notes confirm this reading: "Donations by other group companies (including subsidiaries) must be taken into account in calculating whether the £5,000 threshold has been exceeded."

4.4 Effect of exceeding the threshold. The exemption is partial and severable: "except to the extent that … exceeds £5,000". Worked example — company has made £4,500 of relevant donations in the 12 months before the date of a proposed £1,000 donation; aggregate = £5,500; £500 of the new donation exceeds the threshold and requires authorisation under Part 14; the remaining £500 does not.

4.5 Effect of the exemption on resolutions. Under s. 378(3), a donation exempt under the section is disregarded when determining what donations a resolution passed for the purposes of Part 14 authorises. A resolution is therefore not depleted by exempt donations.

4.6 Legislative history (currency check). The section restates s. 347B of the Companies Act 1985, under which "authorisation for donations is not required unless the donation or aggregate amount of the donations by the company exceeds £5,000 in a 12 month period" (Explanatory Notes, note on s. 378). The figure and the period have not been altered since enactment: the as-enacted text (para. 2.2) and the latest revised text (para. 2.1) are identical in the words of s. 378(1) and the heading. legislation.gov.uk lists only one alternative version ("01/10/2007 – Amendment"), which corresponds to the commencement version point created by S.I. 2007/2194, not to any change in the £5,000 figure or the 12-month period.

5. CURRENCY AGAINST THE 20 NOVEMBER 2026 CUT-OFF

5.1 The instruction posits text "up to date through 20 November 2026". The official revised text retrieved states that s. 378 "is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026" and that "There are changes that may be brought into force at a future date." Because 23 November 2026 is later than 20 November 2026, the retrieved text subsumes the requested cut-off; and because the operative words are unchanged from the as-enacted version, no amendment taking effect between 20 and 23 November 2026 could have altered the answer in any event.
5.2 Residual risk to flag to the reviewer: the retrieved page carries a forward-looking warning of changes not yet in force. Those future changes do not affect the position at 20 November 2026, but the reviewer should re-check the "Changes to legislation" annotation before any answer is given for a date after 20 November 2026.

6. JURISDICTION

6.1 The section carries the extent marker "U.K." and sits in a reserved subject matter (companies), so the same text applies in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The commencement note in para. 2.5 records separate in-force dates for E.W.S. (1 October 2007) and N.I. (1 November 2007) for certain purposes, but the section has been wholly in force throughout the United Kingdom since 1 October 2008.
6.2 For unregistered companies, ss. 362–379 apply with modifications under S.I. 2009/2436 (para. 2.6). If the company secretary's company is an unregistered company, the modified application must be checked separately.
6.3 Nothing in this memorandum addresses the law of any jurisdiction outside the United Kingdom. If the company is subject to another jurisdiction's political-donations regime, this answer does not carry across.

7. WHERE THE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR REQUIRES CHECKING BEFORE RELIANCE

7.1 Definition overlap. Section 364 defines "political donation" for Part 14 by reference to ss. 50–52 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 (see Explanatory Notes, note on s. 364), whereas s. 378(2) supplies its own, differently worded, definition of "donation" for the purposes of the section. The section's own definition is the natural operative definition within s. 378, but the interaction is not spelled out in the text and is the point most likely to matter in a borderline case (for example, a payment that is a "political donation" under s. 364 but not obviously within s. 378(2), or vice versa). Recommend a short note on this before any contested characterisation.
7.2 Date of donation. Section 378(1)(b) turns on "the date on which that donation is made". Section 379 (minor definitions) supplies a construction of references to the date when a donation is made — it is cross-referred to in s. 369(5) as "Section 379(2) (construction of references to date when donation made or expenditure incurred)". The text of s. 379 was not retrieved for this note and should be read before applying the 12-month window to non-cash, indirect or multi-stage donations.
7.3 Scope of the exemption. Section 378 exempts only from the requirement of authorisation under Part 14 (s. 366). It does not address any separate reporting or registration obligation, and no view is expressed on those here.
7.4 Source provenance. The instruction refers to "the text stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026" held by the company secretary. The answer above is taken from the official revised text on legislation.gov.uk. If the secretary's copy is a third-party reproduction, it should be reconciled against the official text before being relied on, particularly as to the heading and subsection (1).

8. SCOPE AND STATUS

8.1 This is a research draft for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and should not be sent to the client in this form.
8.2 It states what s. 378 says. It does not assess whether any particular company's donations are authorised, whether any resolution is adequate, or whether any obligation outside Part 14 applies. Those are separate questions requiring the company's donation history and group structure.

9. ANSWER IN ONE LINE

Section 378 of the Companies Act 2006 (U.K.), as in force on 20 November 2026, sets a ceiling of £5,000 on the aggregate of the donation and other relevant donations made in the period of 12 months ending with the date on which that donation is made; authorisation under Part 14 is not needed except to the extent that aggregate exceeds £5,000.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 37 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/378?view=extent and 378 on legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/pdfs/ukpga_20060046_en_001.pdf. The first reads: "378Donations not amounting to more than £5,000 in any twelve month periodU.K."

question: Y128
answer:
DRAFT MEMORANDUM — FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY. THIS IS NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

1. QUESTION
Before a public company allots shares, what minimum paid-up fraction is stated by section 586 of the Companies Act 2006, using the text stated to be up to date through 20 November 2026?

2. SHORT ANSWER
One-quarter (25%) of the nominal value of each share, plus the whole (100%) of any premium on that share. The statutory words are conjunctive: the share must be paid up at least as to one-quarter of its nominal value AND the whole of any premium on it. Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586(1) (UK).

3. JURISDICTION
United Kingdom. Section 586 is marked 'U.K.' on the official text and sits in Part 17, Chapter 5 ('Additional rules for public companies') of the Companies Act 2006. This answer is confined to that jurisdiction and that statute. It does not state the law of any other jurisdiction.

4. PRIMARY SOURCE AND CURRENCY
Primary source: Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586 (latest available revised text; accessed 23 November 2026). The official page states: 'Companies Act 2006, Section 586 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026. There are changes that may be brought into force at a future date.' Because 23 November 2026 is later than 20 November 2026, that statement covers the requested currency date. The page also carries the version note 'Valid from 01/10/2009' and lists '01/10/2009 - Amendment' among the alternative versions.

Currency check: the operative words of s 586 are the same in (i) the latest available revised text, (ii) the point-in-time version at 26 June 2017 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2017-06-26, accessed 23 November 2026), and (iii) the visible reproduction on LexisNexis (https://www.lexisnexis.co.uk/legal/legislation/uk-parliament-acts/companies-act-2006-c46/part-17/section-586, accessed 23 November 2026) (secondary, paywalled). No amendment to the operative words of s 586 is listed as outstanding. The only 'changes and effects yet to be applied to Section 586' listed on the official page is 'Sch. 11A para. 17E-17G substituted for Sch. 11A para. 17A-17D by 2026 c. 23 Sch. 36 para. 35'; that concerns Schedule 11A and does not alter the words of s 586. The section is also applied by S.I. 2009/1941, art. 12(1), Sch. 3 para. 9 (with art. 10) and S.I. 2011/1265, art. 5(1), Sch. 1 para. 9; those are application provisions, not amendments to the operative text.

5. STATUTORY TEXT
Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586 (UK), headed 'Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up', provides in full:

'586 Public companies: shares must be at least one-quarter paid up

(1) A public company must not allot a share except as paid up at least as to one-quarter of its nominal value and the whole of any premium on it.

(2) This does not apply to shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme.

(3) If a company allots a share in contravention of this section—
(a) the share is to be treated as if one-quarter of its nominal value, together with the whole of any premium on it, had been received, and
(b) the allottee is liable to pay the company the minimum amount which should have been received in respect of the share under subsection (1) (less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up, to any extent, of the share and any premium on it), with interest at the appropriate rate.

(4) Subsection (3) does not apply to the allotment of bonus shares, unless the allottee knew or ought to have known the shares were allotted in contravention of this section.'

6. ANALYSIS
6.1 The minimum fraction. Section 586(1) fixes the floor at 'one-quarter of [the share's] nominal value'. One-quarter is 25%, or 0.25. The fraction is of nominal (par) value, not of the issue price, subscription price, market value or premium-inclusive price. The statutory heading itself says 'at least one-quarter paid up'.

6.2 The premium. The same sentence requires 'the whole of any premium on it'. That is a separate, cumulative requirement: 100% of any premium must be paid up as well as 25% of nominal value. If the share has no premium, the minimum is simply 25% of nominal value. If the share has a premium, the minimum monetary amount is 25% of nominal value plus 100% of the premium. The word 'and' in s 586(1) is conjunctive; satisfaction of the nominal-value element alone is not enough where a premium exists.

6.3 Per-share application. The threshold is expressed by reference to 'a share' in the singular. It must therefore be met for each share allotted, not merely across the allotment as a whole. If different shares have different nominal values or different premiums, the test is applied share by share.

6.4 'Paid up'. For the meaning of 'paid up', see Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 583 (UK). In broad terms, a share is paid up when its nominal value and any premium have been paid up in cash or otherwise; the s 586(1) question is whether the share has been credited as paid up to at least the statutory floor.

6.5 Employees' share scheme exemption. Section 586(2) disapplies the minimum for shares allotted in pursuance of an employees' share scheme. The expression 'employees' share scheme' is defined in Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 1166 (UK). The exemption is specific: it applies to shares allotted in pursuance of such a scheme, not to every allotment to an employee.

6.6 Consequences of contravention. If a public company allots a share in contravention of s 586, s 586(3)(a) treats the share as if one-quarter of its nominal value, together with the whole of any premium, had been received. Section 586(3)(b) makes the allottee liable to pay the company the minimum amount that should have been received under s 586(1), less the value of any consideration actually applied in payment up of the share and any premium, with interest at the appropriate rate. Section 586(4) disapplies s 586(3) for bonus shares unless the allottee knew or ought to have known that the shares were allotted in contravention of the section.

6.7 Public company status. For the definition of 'public company', see Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 4 (UK). A private company limited by shares is not subject to s 586; the section is one of the 'additional rules for public companies'. A company that is not a public company but is re-registered as a public company should ensure that any subsequent allotment complies with s 586.

7. RELATED PUBLIC-COMPANY RULES AFFECTING THE PRACTICAL MINIMUM
Section 586 does not stand alone. The following provisions in the same Chapter may affect how the s 586(1) floor is satisfied in practice:

7.1 Section 584 (public companies: shares taken by subscribers of memorandum). 'Shares taken by a subscriber to the memorandum of a public company in pursuance of an undertaking of his in the memorandum, and any premium on the shares, must be paid up in cash.' Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 584 (UK).

7.2 Section 585 (public companies: must not accept undertaking to do work or perform services). 'A public company must not accept at any time, in payment up of its shares or any premium on them, an undertaking given by any person that he or another should do work or perform services for the company or any other person.' Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 585(1) (UK).

7.3 Section 587 (public companies: payment by long-term undertaking). 'A public company must not allot shares as fully or partly paid up (as to their nominal value or any premium on them) otherwise than in cash if the consideration for the allotment is or includes an undertaking which is to be, or may be, performed more than five years after the date of the allotment.' Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 587(1) (UK).

7.4 Sections 593–597 (public companies: valuation of non-cash consideration). A public company must not allot shares as fully or partly paid up otherwise than in cash unless the consideration for the allotment has been valued in accordance with those sections. Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), ss 593–597 (UK). The s 586(1) threshold is not avoided by using non-cash consideration; the valuation rules operate alongside it.

7.5 Section 580 (shares not to be allotted at a discount). 'A company's shares must not be allotted at a discount.' Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 580(1) (UK). This is a separate prohibition and does not alter the s 586(1) fraction.

8. PRACTICAL APPLICATION
8.1 No premium. If a public company allots a £1 nominal share at par, the minimum paid-up amount is £0.25 per share (25% of £1). If it allots 1,000 such shares, the aggregate minimum paid-up amount is £250.

8.2 With premium. If a public company allots a £1 nominal share at £5, the premium is £4. The minimum paid-up amount is £0.25 (25% of £1 nominal) plus £4 (100% of the premium) = £4.25 per share. For 1,000 shares, the aggregate minimum is £4,250. The statutory fraction of nominal value remains one-quarter; the premium is an additional statutory amount, not a percentage of nominal value.

8.3 Non-cash consideration. If the shares are to be paid up by non-cash consideration, the company must still ensure that the consideration actually applied results in the share being paid up to at least 25% of nominal value plus 100% of any premium, and must comply with the valuation requirements in ss 593–597.

8.4 Articles may require more. Section 586(1) is a statutory floor. The company's articles, the allotment contract or the terms of issue may require a higher paid-up amount; s 586 does not prevent that.

9. VERIFICATION AND AUTHORITY
No conflicting versions of the operative words of s 586 were found. The latest available revised text, the 26 June 2017 point-in-time text and the visible commercial reproduction all contain the same s 586(1) sentence. The official 'Changes to Legislation' note records only future or outstanding changes; the one listed for the section page concerns Schedule 11A, not s 586. The statutory language is clear and no judicial decision is necessary to answer the textual question. If a dispute arose, a court would construe the ordinary meaning of 'one-quarter of its nominal value' and 'the whole of any premium' in the usual way. Authority is not thin on the point; the only practical caution is to apply the test per share and to add the whole premium, not to treat 25% of the issue price as the statutory fraction.

10. CITATIONS
Primary source:
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586 (UK), https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586 (latest available revised text; stated up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026; accessed 23 November 2026).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586(1) (UK) (the operative minimum).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586(2) (UK) (employees' share scheme exemption).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586(3) (UK) (consequences of contravention).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586(4) (UK) (bonus shares).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 4 (UK) (definition of public company).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 583 (UK) (meaning of paid up).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 584 (UK) (subscribers' shares to be paid in cash).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 585 (UK) (no undertaking to do work or perform services).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 587 (UK) (long-term undertakings).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), ss 593–597 (UK) (valuation of non-cash consideration).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 580 (UK) (no allotment at a discount).
- Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 1166 (UK) (definition of employees' share scheme).

Official page history and application:
- Companies Act 2006, s 586, point-in-time version at 26 June 2017, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/46/section/586/2017-06-26 (accessed 23 November 2026).
- Companies Act 2006 (Consequential Amendments, Transitional Provisions and Savings) Order 2009 (S.I. 2009/1941), art. 12(1), Sch. 3 para. 9 (with art. 10).
- Companies Act 2006 (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Order 2011 (S.I. 2011/1265), art. 5(1), Sch. 1 para. 9.

Secondary corroboration (not relied on as authority):
- LexisNexis, Companies Act 2006 (2006 c. 46), s 586, https://www.lexisnexis.co.uk/legal/legislation/uk-parliament-acts/companies-act-2006-c46/part-17/section-586 (accessed 23 November 2026) (paywalled reproduction; visible words match the official text).

11. CAVEATS
This memorandum is a draft for review by a qualified attorney and is not legal advice. It answers only the textual question under s 586 of the Companies Act 2006 as stated to be current through 20 November 2026. It does not address tax, listing rules, financial services regulation, foreign law, or the constitutional documents of any particular company. If the entity is not a UK public company, or if the allotment is pursuant to an employees' share scheme, or if the consideration is non-cash, the analysis must be checked against the specific facts and the related provisions identified above.

question: Y129
answer:
DRAFT FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

MEMORANDUM

Re: Word limits on memoranda supporting or opposing motions in an FTC adjudicative proceeding under 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on 21 November 2026
Jurisdiction: United States — federal administrative adjudication before the Federal Trade Commission under the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. §§ 41–58; procedural rules codified at 16 C.F.R. Part 3.

I. QUESTION PRESENTED

In an adjudicative proceeding governed by 16 C.F.R. Part 3, as that Part stood on 21 November 2026, what word limits apply to (a) memoranda supporting or opposing a dispositive motion and (b) memoranda supporting or opposing any other motion?

II. SHORT ANSWER

The unit is WORDS, not pages. Both limits sit in a single provision, 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) ("Content").

| Motion paper | Limit | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Memorandum in support of, or in opposition to, a DISPOSITIVE motion | 10,000 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) |
| Memorandum in support of, or in opposition to, ANY OTHER motion | 2,500 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) |
| Reply in support of a dispositive motion (adjacent, for completeness) | 5,000 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) |
| Reply in support of any other motion authorized by the ALJ or the Commission (adjacent) | 1,250 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) |
| Memorandum in support of/opposition to a motion under § 3.26 (motions following denial of preliminary injunctive relief) | 10,000 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.26(e) |
| Application for review and answer under § 3.23 (interlocutory appeal — not a motion memorandum, listed to prevent misapplication) | 2,500 words | 16 C.F.R. § 3.23(c) |

Answers in one line: 10,000 words for a dispositive-motion memorandum; 2,500 words for a memorandum on any other motion.

III. OPERATIVE TEXT (QUOTED)

16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c) provides, in relevant part:

"All written motions shall state the particular order, ruling, or action desired and the grounds therefor. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion shall not exceed 10,000 words. Memoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion shall not exceed 2,500 words. Any reply in support of a dispositive motion shall not exceed 5,000 words and any reply in support of any other motion authorized by the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission shall not exceed 1,250 words. These word count limitations include headings, footnotes, and quotations, but do not include the cover, table of contents, table of citations or authorities, glossaries, statements with respect to oral argument, any addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations, any certificates of counsel, proposed form of order, and any attachment required by § 3.45(e). Documents that fail to comply with these provisions shall not be filed with the Secretary."

(16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c), as set out in the 1 January 2023 edition of the Code of Federal Regulations, 16 C.F.R. ch. I, and carried in the govinfo XML of that section; source strings in Part IX below.)

IV. ANALYSIS

A. Dispositive motions — 10,000 words. Section 3.22(c) caps "[m]emoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any dispositive motion" at 10,000 words. The cap is symmetrical: it applies identically to the moving party's supporting memorandum and the opposing party's opposition memorandum. There is no separate page limit in § 3.22.

B. Any other motion — 2,500 words. The same sentence structure caps "[m]emoranda in support of, or in opposition to, any other motion" at 2,500 words, again symmetrically as between movant and opponent. "Any other motion" is the residual category: everything that is not dispositive. That includes, by way of illustration, discovery motions (to compel or determine sufficiency, § 3.38(a); to quash, § 3.34(c)), motions for sanctions (§ 3.38(b)), motions for enforcement (§ 3.38(c)), motions in limine, and motions for extensions of time. Note that the discovery motions just listed carry an additional, non-length requirement: a signed meet-and-confer statement under § 3.22(g).

C. What counts toward the limit — identical across all four caps. The rule expressly includes headings, footnotes, and quotations in the count. It expressly excludes: the cover; table of contents; table of citations or authorities; glossaries; statements with respect to oral argument; addendums containing statutes, rules or regulations; certificates of counsel; the proposed form of order; and any attachment required by § 3.45(e) (in camera filings). A drafter should therefore not attempt to escape the cap by moving substance into footnotes — footnotes are counted.

D. Enforcement consequence. Section 3.22(c) is self-executing at the filing office: "Documents that fail to comply with these provisions shall not be filed with the Secretary." An over-length memorandum is subject to rejection, not merely to a scolding.

E. No general waiver. Section 3.22(f) permits the Administrative Law Judge or the Commission to "waive the requirements of this section as to motions for extensions of time" only. That is a narrow carve-out; it is not authority to waive the word caps for other motion types. Relief from an over-length filing must therefore be sought by leave or by case-specific order, not under § 3.22(f).

F. Summary decision is routed through § 3.22(c), not through a bespoke cap. 16 C.F.R. § 3.24 (summary decision) — as captured in the sources reviewed — contains no word-count provision; its text addresses affidavits, the opposing party's inability to present facts, partial summary decision, and bad-faith affidavits. A motion for summary decision is, in substance, a dispositive motion, so its supporting and opposing memoranda fall under the 10,000-word cap in § 3.22(c). See the caveat at VII.B below on the absence of a definition.

G. Motions under § 3.26 have their own 10,000-word cap. 16 C.F.R. § 3.26 (motions following denial of preliminary injunctive relief) sets its own limit in paragraph (e): "Memoranda in support of or in opposition to motions authorized by this section shall not exceed 10,000 words," with the same inclusion/exclusion list as § 3.22(c). The number coincides with the § 3.22(c) dispositive figure, but the source of the cap is § 3.26(e), and a § 3.26 motion should be sized against that provision.

H. Adjacent limits that are frequently confused with motion limits. (i) Section 3.23(c): neither an application for review of an interlocutory ruling nor the answer to it "shall exceed 2,500 words," using the same inclusion/exclusion list, and the Commission may order additional briefing. (ii) Reply briefs: 5,000 words (dispositive) and 1,250 words (other motions), § 3.22(c). (iii) Section 3.23(a)(2) contemplates that a Commission order placing a matter on review "will make provision for the filing of memoranda of law if deemed appropriate by the Commission" — where the Commission sets that briefing, its order, not § 3.22(c), controls length.

V. PROCEDURAL POSTURE — WHAT THE ANSWER ASSUMES

The figures above are the Part 3 default limits. They assume (i) no case-specific scheduling or case-management order in the particular proceeding sets different limits; (ii) the question concerns motion papers rather than prehearing or post-hearing briefs (a different question under Part 3); and (iii) the question concerns written memoranda rather than oral argument. Each assumption should be checked against the docket before a filing is sized. A presiding Administrative Law Judge's scheduling order controls the proceeding before that judge, and § 3.23(a)(2) and § 3.23(c) expressly contemplate Commission-set briefing in the interlocutory context.

VI. PRACTICAL COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST

1. Classify the motion first: dispositive (10,000) versus other (2,500). Classification drives a 4x difference in allowance.
2. If the motion is under § 3.26, cite § 3.26(e) (10,000) rather than § 3.22(c).
3. Count headings, footnotes, and quotations. Do not count the cover, TOC, table of authorities, glossary, oral-argument statement, statutory/regulatory addendum, certificate of counsel, proposed form of order, or § 3.45(e) attachments.
4. Attach a word count; the rule's exclusion list is specific enough that a bare assertion is risky.
5. Confirm the proposed form of order is attached — § 3.22(c) requires "a draft order containing the proposed relief" — and that counsel's name, address, telephone, fax, and e-mail appear on the motion.
6. If the motion is a discovery motion of the kind listed in § 3.22(g), attach the signed meet-and-confer statement.
7. Budget the reply separately: 5,000 or 1,250 words, filed within 5 days after service of the last answer.
8. If the substance will not fit, do not plan on § 3.22(f); seek leave or a case-specific order.

VII. WHERE THE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR NEEDS RE-VERIFICATION

A. Point-in-time verification of § 3.22(c) as of 21 November 2026. The verbatim word-count text quoted in Part III is taken from the 1 January 2023 CFR edition of § 3.22 and the corresponding govinfo XML/PDF. The eCFR "current" fetch of § 3.22 (retrieved 23 November 2026) captured paragraphs (b), (e), (f), and (g), which are textually identical to the 2023 edition — indicating the section's structure is unchanged — but the captured passages did not include paragraph (c) itself. Before relying on the figures for a filing, confirm § 3.22(c) in the eCFR point-in-time view for 21 November 2026 and confirm no Federal Register amendment to Part 3 took effect between the 2023 edition and that date. The 2015 amendments at 80 Fed. Reg. 15160 (Mar. 23, 2015) are the source of the word-count regime reflected in the 2023 text; § 3.22 itself carries the history note "[74 FR 1821, Jan. 13, 2009, as amended at 80 FR 15160, Mar. 23, 2015]."

B. "Dispositive motion" is not defined in Part 3. No definition appears in the provisions reviewed. The classification of a summary-decision motion (or of a motion to dismiss at the close of the evidence, referenced in § 3.22(a)) as dispositive is a reasoned inference from the structure of Part 3 — § 3.24 sets no independent cap, and a summary-decision motion seeks termination of the case — rather than the product of an express definition. If a filing is near the 2,500-word line and the motion's character is arguable, the safe course is to size to 2,500 or to seek leave to file at greater length.

C. Case-specific orders. Part 3 limits are defaults. Nothing reviewed forecloses a presiding judge from setting different limits by order in a particular proceeding, and the interlocutory-review provisions expressly contemplate Commission-ordered briefing.

D. Scope. This memorandum addresses only 16 C.F.R. Part 3 (FTC adjudication). Word-limit rules of other agencies' adjudicative processes, and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, do not carry over.

VIII. CONCLUSION

For an FTC adjudicative proceeding under 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on 21 November 2026, the word limits are: 10,000 words for a memorandum in support of or in opposition to a dispositive motion; 2,500 words for a memorandum in support of or in opposition to any other motion. Both limits are in 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(c), include headings, footnotes, and quotations, exclude the front matter and attachments specified in the rule, and are enforced by the Secretary's refusal to file noncompliant documents.

IX. SOURCES CITED IN FULL

Text consulted in the Code of Federal Regulations, 16 C.F.R. ch. I (1 January 2023 edition), govinfo XML, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title16-vol1/xml/CFR-2023-title16-vol1-sec3-22.xml (fetched 2026-11-23); govinfo PDF, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2023-title16-vol1/pdf/CFR-2023-title16-vol1-sec3-22.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23); and eCFR, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/part-3/section-3.22 and https://ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3/subpart-C/section-3.22 (fetched 2026-11-23).
2. 16 C.F.R. § 3.23 ("Interlocutory appeals"), including § 3.23(a)(2), (b), (c) (2,500-word cap on applications for review and answers), (d), (e). https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3/subpart-C/section-3.23 (fetched 2026-11-23).
3. 16 C.F.R. § 3.24 ("Summary decision"), including § 3.24(a)(4), (a)(5), and (b). https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-3/subpart-C (fetched 2026-11-23).

7. Rules of Practice amendments, 80 Fed. Reg. 15160 (Mar. 23, 2015) (source of the word-count regime in § 3.22 and § 3.26).

question: Y130
answer:
WITHDRAWAL PERIOD UNDER DIRECTIVE 2011/83/EU — DRAFTING NOTE AND DRAFT WITHDRAWAL INSTRUCTIONS

Prepared for attorney review. Draft, not legal advice. Jurisdiction: European Union — Directive 2011/83/EU on consumer rights, OJ L 304, 22.11.2011, p. 64-88, as consolidated (CELEX 02011L0083-20260927), cited to the request. It governs where a trader directs distance contracts to consumers in a Member State. If the retailer also targets consumers in the United Kingdom, the Directive has not applied there since 31 December 2020 and the domestic transposition (Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, SI 2013/3134, as amended) governs instead — to be checked before the notice is published in that market.

1. SHORT ANSWER

1.1 Service contract — Article 9(2)(a): the period of 14 days expires 14 days from the day of the conclusion of the contract. Article 9(1) (quoted): “the consumer shall have a period of 14 days to withdraw from a distance or off-premises contract, without giving any reason, and without incurring any costs other than those provided for in Article 13(2) and Article 14.” Article 9(2) (quoted): “Without prejudice to Article 10, the withdrawal period referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall expire after 14 days from: (a) in the case of service contracts, the day of the conclusion of the contract.”

1.2 Sales contract — Article 9(2)(b): the period of 14 days expires 14 days from the day on which the consumer, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer, acquires physical possession of the goods. Quoted: “(b) in the case of sales contracts, the day on which the consumer or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by the consumer acquires physical possession of the goods or: (i)…” The period does not run from conclusion, from payment or from dispatch — only from physical possession.

1.3 Both limbs are subject to Article 10 (omission of the information on the right of withdrawal). If the trader has not given the consumer the information required by Article 6(1)(h), the period expires 12 months from the end of the initial period as determined under Article 9(2) (Article 10(1), quoted). If that information is given within those 12 months, the period expires 14 days after the day on which the consumer receives it (Article 10(2), quoted). Example: service concluded 4 March 2026, no information — initial period ends 18 March 2026, extended period ends 18 March 2027; information delivered 10 June 2026 — period ends 24 June 2026.

1.4 Figures stated once and used consistently throughout: base period 14 days (both limbs); extension 12 months measured from the end of that 14-day period; restart 14 days from receipt of the late information. No other period is asserted.

2. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE THE EXPIRY DATE

2.1 Requesting performance of a service during the period does not shorten it. The period under Article 9(2)(a) still runs from conclusion; the request affects only the consequences — the consumer pays a proportionate amount for what has been supplied up to the communication of withdrawal (Article 14(3)) [V], and the right is lost only once the service has been fully performed, where performance began with the consumer's prior express agreement and acknowledgment of the loss of the right (Article 16(a)) [V].

2.2 A term of the contract or of the notice that shortens or waives the period is not binding: Article 25 (quoted): “Any contractual terms which directly or indirectly waive or restrict the rights resulting from this Directive shall not be binding on the consumer.” The 14-day period is a maximum-harmonisation floor for distance contracts and cannot be shortened by national transposition (Article 4) [V].

2.3 Multi-item deliveries — Article 9(2)(b)(i)-(iii) [V, the fetched text truncates at “(i)”]: several goods ordered in one order and delivered separately — period runs from possession of the last good; goods consisting of multiple lots or pieces — from the last lot or piece; regular delivery over a defined period — from possession of the first good. To be verified against the OJ text before the notice goes live, because it decides the date for split deliveries.

3. THE ONE OPEN NATIONAL POINT: DAY-COUNTING (does not change the 14-day period)

3.1 The Directive fixes the length at 14 days but not the convention for counting the trigger day. National civil-law computation rules decide whether the day of conclusion / of possession is day 1 or day 0. Two workt examples (trigger 4 March 2026):
  (a) trigger day not counted — period runs 5-18 March, expires at the end of 18 March 2026;
  (b) trigger day counted as day 1 — expires at the end of 17 March 2026.
Same one-day spread for the sales limb and for the Article 10(2) restart. Recommendation: the notice should not hard-code a date; it should state the rule (“from the day of…”, “at the end of the fourteenth day thereafter”) and, where the retailer displays a calculated date, calculate it under the law of the Member State of the consumer. Confirmation of the applicable national computation rule is the only item left open, and it is a date, not the period.

4. DRAFT WITHDRAWAL INSTRUCTIONS (for publication on the website and on a durable medium after conclusion; modelled on Annex I(A)-(B)) [Annex text: V]

“RIGHT OF WITHDRAWAL
You have the right to withdraw from this contract without giving any reason within 14 days.

When the withdrawal period expires
— Service contract (e.g. [subscription / installation / cleaning]): the 14-day period starts on the day on which the contract is concluded and expires at the end of the fourteenth day thereafter.
— Sales contract (goods): the 14-day period starts on the day on which you, or a third party other than the carrier and indicated by you, acquire physical possession of the goods, and expires at the end of the fourteenth day thereafter. Where your order comprises several goods delivered separately, the period starts on the day on which you acquire physical possession of the last good. Where the contract provides for the regular delivery of goods over a defined period, the period starts on the day on which you acquire physical possession of the first good.
To respect the deadline, it is sufficient that you send your communication concerning the exercise of the right of withdrawal before the expiry of the withdrawal period.

EXERCISING THE RIGHT OF WITHDRAWAL
To exercise the right of withdrawal, you must inform us, [TRADER NAME], [GEOGRAPHICAL ADDRESS], [TELEPHONE], [E-MAIL], of your decision to withdraw from this contract by an unequivocal statement (for example a letter sent by post or an e-mail). You may use the model withdrawal form below, but it is not obligatory.

MODEL WITHDRAWAL FORM (Annex I(B))
To [TRADER NAME, GEOGRAPHICAL ADDRESS, E-MAIL]: I/We hereby give notice that I/we withdraw from my/our contract for the sale of the following goods / for the supply of the following service: — Ordered on / received on: — Name of consumer(s): — Address of consumer(s): — Signature of consumer(s) (only if this form is notified on paper): — Date.

EFFECTS OF WITHDRAWAL
[Reimboursement of all payments received, including the costs of delivery (other than supplementary costs arising from a delivery method other than the least expensive standard delivery offered), without undue delay and in any event within 14 days from the day on which we are informed of the decision to withdraw; reimboursement by the same means of payment as used in the initial transaction, unless you expressly agree otherwise and provided you incur no fees as a result. Article 13(1)-(2).] [V]
[Where you withdraw from a sales contract, you return the goods without undue delay and in any event within 14 days from your communication of withdrawal; you bear the direct cost of returning the goods. Article 14(1).] [V]
[Where you have requested the performance of the service during the withdrawal period, you shall pay an amount proportionate to what has been supplied up to the moment you informed us of your withdrawal. Article 14(3).] [V]
[You bear no cost for the performance of the service during the withdrawal period where we have not given you the information on the right of withdrawal under Article 6(1)(h) or where you did not expressly request performance before the end of the 14-day period. Article 14(4)(a).] [V]”

5. DRAFTING NOTES FOR THE REVIEWER

5.1 Do not print a fixed number of days other than 14, and do not print a calendar date that assumes one counting convention for all markets (paragraph 3).
5.2 The service limb must not be described as running from the start of performance, from the first invoice or from the end of the contract — Article 9(2)(a) says conclusion.
5.3 The sales limb must not be described as running from dispatch, from conclusion or from payment.
5.4 The notice should tell the consumer that the period is extended (12 months; or 14 days from receipt of the information) if the required information was omitted or given late — Article 10. Silence here is the fact pattern that triggers Article 10 against the trader.
5.5 Record the day of conclusion (service) and the day of physical possession, with carrier tracking (sales); the extension and restart periods under Article 10 are computed from those dates.
5.6 Correction to the project plan's mapping (the plan is not the instrument): the 14-day service period is Article 9(2)(a), not Article 6(1); the sales period is Article 9(2)(b), not Article 7(1)-(2); the extensions and restarts are Article 10, not Article 7(3)-(6); Article 7 concerns formal requirements for off-premises contracts; Article 10 is omission of information, not burden of proof. The plan's substantive instincts (14 days; service from conclusion; sales from possession; 12-month fallback) were right and are carried forward unchanged.

6. VERIFICATION SCHEDULE (cited in substance above; not in the fetched excerpt)
[V] Article 2(5) definition of sales contract (including mixed goods-and-services contracts treated as sales); Article 4 level of harmonisation; Article 6(1)(h) content of the withdrawal information; Article 9(2)(b)(i)-(iii) multi-item rules; Article 13(1)-(2) reimboursement; Article 14(1), (3), (4)(a) costs and pro-rata charge; Article 16(a) full performance of a service; Annex I(A)-(B) model instructions and form. Quoted in full above and therefore not on this schedule: Articles 9(1), 9(2)(a)-(b), 10(1)-(2), 11(1), 25.

question: Y131
answer:
MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

Subject: The presumption applicable to everyone charged with a criminal offence under the European Convention on Human Rights, in the text as amended through Protocol No. 15
Jurisdiction / legal order: Council of Europe — the international treaty system of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and the supervisory jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). No domestic legal order is addressed; how the Convention operates inside any State Party depends on that State's implementing legislation and is outside this note.
Prepared for: fair-trial training module.

=====================================================================
I. QUESTION PRESENTED
=====================================================================
What presumption does the European Convention on Human Rights, in the text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15, apply to everyone charged with a criminal offence?

=====================================================================
II. SHORT ANSWER
=====================================================================
The presumption of innocence. Article 6(2) ECHR provides, in the authentic English text:

    "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."

That single sentence is the whole of Article 6(2). The provision is unchanged by Protocol No. 15; the consolidated text amended through Protocol No. 15 reads identically at Article 6(2) to the text as it stood on 4 November 1950.

=====================================================================
III. THE GOVERNING TEXT — VERBATIM, WITH IMMEDIATE CONTEXT
=====================================================================
Reproduced exactly as it appears in the official Court publication (source at Part IV), including the Convention's British spelling ("offence", "proved", not "proven"):

ARTICLE 6
Right to a fair trial

1. In the determination of his civil rights and obligations or of any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. Judgment shall be pronounced publicly but the press and public may be excluded from all or part of the trial in the interests of morals, public order or national security in a democratic society, where the interests of juveniles or the protection of the private life of the parties so require, or to the extent strictly necessary in the opinion of the court in special circumstances where publicity would prejudice the interests of justice.

2. Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.

3. Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights:
   (a) to be informed promptly, in a language which he understands and in detail, of the nature and cause of the accusation against him;
   (b) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence;
   (c) to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be given it free when the interests of justice so require;
   (d) to examine or have examined witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him;
   (e) to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court.

[Article 6(1) and 6(3) are set out above only as context. The operative answer to the question is Article 6(2). Article 6(3) intro and sub-paragraphs (a)-(e) are the standard text; verify lettering against the source before printing in the module — see Part X, item 6.]

=====================================================================
IV. PRIMARY SOURCE, CITED IN FULL
=====================================================================
Controlling instrument (consolidated text):

  Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, opened for signature 4 November 1950, Rome, ETS No. 005, 213 U.N.T.S. 221 (entered into force 3 September 1953), as amended by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155), Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) and Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213), Article 6(2).

Text consulted (official publication of the European Court of Human Rights, English version), "European Convention on Human Rights" — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (retrieved 23 November 2026; document hash sha256 f4608f7ed2d5). The relevant passage reads: "ARTICLE 6 / Right to a fair trial / 1. ... / 2. Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law. / 3. Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights:".

Amending instrument:

  Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Strasbourg, 24 June 2013, CETS No. 213 (entered into force 1 August 2021).

  Text consulted: https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Protocol_15_ENG (retrieved 23 November 2026; sha256 57f7f5bb1c0e).
  Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213): https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng (retrieved 23 November 2026; sha256 d85a250bb703).
  Entry into force corroborated by: Netherlands Treaty Database, Treaty No. 012860, Protocol No. 15 ("Entry into force 01-08-2021"), https://verdragenbank.overheid.nl/en/Treaty/Details/012860.html (retrieved 23 November 2026; sha256 d57d2011914c).

Secondary / official Court research aid (cited as such, not as authority):
  ECtHR Knowledge Sharing, "Presumption of innocence" (Key Theme, Article 6 criminal), https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/presumption-of-innocence (retrieved 23 November 2026; sha256 11513bbf5174).

=====================================================================
V. CONFIRMATION THAT THE CITED TEXT IS THE TEXT AMENDED THROUGH PROTOCOL No. 15
=====================================================================
This is the point on which the third constraint turns, and it can be demonstrated from the documents themselves rather than assumed.

1. Protocol No. 15, Article 1, replaces the preamble of the Convention with, inter alia, the following new paragraph (quoted from the Protocol text):

   "Affirming that the High Contracting Parties, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, have the primary responsibility to secure the rights and freedoms defined in this Convention and the Protocols thereto, and that in doing so they enjoy a margin of appreciation, subject to the supervisory jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights established by this Convention,"

2. That exact paragraph appears in the preamble of the consolidated English text at the source cited in Part IV ("Affirming that the High Contracting Parties, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, have the primary responsibility to secure the rights and freedoms defined in this Convention and the Protocols thereto, and that in doing so they enjoy a margin of appreciation, subject to the supervisory jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights established by this Convention,").

3. Therefore the text at Part IV is, on its face, the consolidated text incorporating Protocol No. 15 — not a pre-2021 print. This is the internal consistency check that satisfies constraint (3).

4. Protocol No. 15 entered into force on 1 August 2021 (Netherlands Treaty Database, Treaty No. 012860), so the consolidated text post-dating that date is the "as amended through Protocol No. 15" text.

=====================================================================
VI. PROTOCOL No. 15 DID NOT AMEND ARTICLE 6
=====================================================================
The operative provisions of Protocol No. 15 amend the following provisions of the Convention, and no others:

  - Article 1 of the Protocol — the preamble (inserting the subsidiarity / margin of appreciation paragraph quoted at Part V). Confirmed by the Protocol text.
  - Article 2 of the Protocol — Article 21 (inserting a new paragraph 2: candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates is requested; renumbering) and Article 23 (deleting paragraph 2 and renumbering). Confirmed by the Protocol text and by Article 8(1) of the Protocol (transitional provision referring to lists submitted under Article 22).
  - Article 3 of the Protocol — Article 30 (deleting the words "unless one of the parties to the case objects"). Confirmed by the Protocol text and by Article 8(2) of the Protocol (transitional provision referring to relinquishment in favour of the Grand Chamber).
  - Article 4 of the Protocol — Article 35(1) (the time limit for applications). Confirmed by Article 8(3) of the Protocol: "Article 4 of this Protocol shall enter into force following the expiration of a period of six months after the date of entry into force of this Protocol. Article 4 of this Protocol shall not apply to applications in respect of which the final decision within the meaning of Article 35, paragraph 1 of the Convention was taken prior to the date of entry into force of Article 4 ..."
  - Article 5 of the Protocol — also an amendment to Article 35 (admissibility). The full text of Article 5 of the Protocol was not reproduced in the material consulted; see Part X, item 5.
  - Articles 6 to 9 of the Protocol — final and transitional clauses (the Explanatory Report describes Articles 6 and 7 as standard final clauses, Article 8 as transitional provisions, and Article 9 as a standard final clause).

No article of Protocol No. 15 refers to Article 6, to Article 6(2), or to the presumption of innocence. The Explanatory Report contains no reference to Article 6 in connection with any amendment. Accordingly, Article 6(2) in the consolidated text is textually identical to the 1950 text, and the answer to the question does not depend on which pre- or post-Protocol No. 15 print is consulted — but the module should nonetheless cite the consolidated text, as instructed.

Practical consequence for the training module: it is accurate, and useful, to say expressly that Protocol No. 15 left Article 6(2) untouched. That forecloses the learner's natural but wrong inference that "as amended through Protocol No. 15" means the presumption itself was reformulated in 2021.

=====================================================================
VII. SCOPE OF "EVERYONE CHARGED WITH A CRIMINAL OFFENCE"
=====================================================================
Article 6(2) is not confined by the label used in national law. "Criminal charge" is an autonomous Convention concept, determined by reference to (i) the classification in domestic law, (ii) the nature of the offence, and (iii) the nature and severity of the penalty — Engel and Others v. the Netherlands, 8 June 1976, Series A no. 22, §§ 82-83 (verify paragraph numbers in HUDOC before publication). A domestic disciplinary or administrative label therefore does not by itself displace Article 6(2).

The Court's own research aid states the two aspects of Article 6(2) as follows (quoted from the ECtHR Knowledge Sharing page cited in Part IV): "As a procedural guarantee in the context of a criminal trial itself where it imposes requirements in respect of, inter alia, the burden of proof; legal presumptions of fact and law; the privilege against self-incrimination; pre-trial publicity; and premature expressions, by the trial court or by other public officials, of a defendant's guilt; and ... As a guarantee to protect individuals who have been acquitted of a criminal charge, or in respect of whom criminal proceedings have been discontinued, from being treated by public officials and authorities as though they are in fact guilty of the offence charged." The page attributes these two aspects to Allen v. the United Kingdom [GC], 2013, §§ 93-94, and Nealon and Hallam v. the United Kingdom [GC], 2024, § 109.

=====================================================================
VIII. ARTICLE 6(2) IS DISTINCT FROM ARTICLE 6(3)
=====================================================================
Article 6(2) states the presumption. Article 6(3) states the "minimum rights" of everyone charged with a criminal offence and is a separate paragraph with its own introductory words. The module should not present the Article 6(3) guarantees as part of the presumption; they are related fair-trial guarantees, not components of Article 6(2).

=====================================================================
IX. WHAT THE PRESUMPTION REQUIRES — TRAINING POINTS, EACH TIED TO A SOURCE
=====================================================================
Include these only if the module is meant to go beyond the bare text (the request asks for "the exact presumption", so Parts II-IV are the deliverable and this Part is optional enrichment):

1. Burden of proof on the prosecution; doubt benefits the accused. Barberà, Messegué and Jabardo v. Spain, 6 December 1988, Series A no. 146, § 77 ("Article 6 § 2 ... requires, inter alia, that, when carrying out their duties, the members of a court should not start with the preconceived idea that the accused has committed the offence charged; the burden of proof is on the prosecution, and any doubt should benefit the accused.") — verify § 77 against HUDOC.
2. Presumptions of fact or law are not as such prohibited, but must be confined within reasonable limits and the means of defence must be preserved. Salabiaku v. France, 7 October 1988, Series A no. 141-A, § 28 — verify.
3. Judicial or official statements of guilt before proof. From the ECtHR Knowledge Sharing page (Part IV): "A breach of the presumption of innocence will occur if a judicial decision concerning an accused person reflects an opinion of guilt before being proven guilty according to law. It suffices, even in the absence of any formal finding, that there is some reasoning suggesting that the court regards the accused as guilty (Gutsanovi v. Bulgaria, 2013, §§ 202-203)." Also: "the lack of intention to breach the right to the presumption of innocence cannot rule out a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention (Avaz Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan, 2021, § 69)", and "it is always important to take into account the true meaning of the statements in question, rather than their literal form (Lavents v. Latvia, 2002, § 126)".
4. Acquittal does not end the protection: "The fact that the applicant is ultimately found guilty does not negate his initial right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law (Matijašević v. Serbia, 2006, § 49 ...)" — ECtHR Knowledge Sharing page, Part IV.
5. Pre-trial publicity requires balancing Articles 6 and 10: "A balancing of rights under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention is necessary in order to guarantee both a fair hearing and freedom of expression (Bédat v. Switzerland [GC], 2016, § 51)" — ECtHR Knowledge Sharing page, Part IV.
6. Silence and self-incrimination: "The right to remain silent and the privilege against self-incrimination, as implied aspects of a fair trial, are closely linked to the presumption of innocence. The prosecution in a criminal case must seek to prove their case against an accused without resort to evidence obtained through methods of coercion or oppression in defiance of the will of the accused (Heaney and McGuinness v. Ireland, 2000, § 40)" — ECtHR Knowledge Sharing page, Part IV; see also O'Halloran and Francis v. the United Kingdom [GC], 2007, § 55 (compliance depends on the nature and degree of compulsion, the safeguards, and the use made of the material).

=====================================================================
X. WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN, CONFLICTING, OR NEEDS VERIFICATION BEFORE USE
=====================================================================
1. Article 6(2) itself: no thinness or conflict. The text is settled, single-sentence, and unamended since 1950. This is the only point the answer strictly depends on.
2. The paragraph numbers of the ECtHR judgments cited in Part IX were taken from the Court's own Knowledge Sharing summary page, not from the judgments themselves. Before the module prints any of them, pull each judgment from HUDOC (hudoc.echr.coe.int) and confirm the paragraph number and the quotation. Treat Part IX citations as unverified until that check is done.
3. Engel v. the Netherlands, Barberà and Salabiaku citations in Part IX were supplied from general knowledge of the case law, not from the fetched material. Verify in HUDOC before publication.
4. Correction to the instruction's assumptions: the project note refers to an "Article 6(2) second sentence on pre-trial publicity". There is no second sentence. Article 6(2) is one sentence. Pre-trial publicity is a case-law gloss on that single sentence, not a separate textual limb. The module must not tell learners otherwise.
5. The full text of Article 5 of Protocol No. 15 was not reproduced in the material consulted; the description at Part VI of Articles 4 and 5 as amendments to Article 35 rests on the Protocol's Article 8(3) transitional provision (fetched) for Article 4, and on the known structure of the Protocol for Article 5. This does not affect the answer, because no article of the Protocol touches Article 6. If the module will describe Protocol No. 15's contents in detail, obtain the full CETS No. 213 text from the Council of Europe Treaty Office and confirm Articles 4 and 5.
6. The Article 6(3) lettering in Part III is standard but was truncated in the fetched passage ("3. Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights:"). If Article 6(3) is printed in the module, verify sub-paragraphs (a)-(e) against the source document.
7. Language version: only the English text was consulted. The Convention is authentic in English and French (ETS No. 005, final provisions). If the module is bilingual, obtain the French authentic text from the Treaty Office and use it, not a translation. The English and French texts are equally authentic; a divergence between them would be a matter for the Court's interpretive practice, not for a training slide.
8. Domestic effect: this note says nothing about how Article 6(2) is given effect in any particular State Party (for example, in the United Kingdom, via the Human Rights Act 1998, Schedule 1). If the audience is domestic, that is a separate question requiring separate authority.
9. The UNTS citation (213 U.N.T.S. 221) is the conventional registration citation and should be confirmed against the UN Treaty Series before it is printed in any citation table.

=====================================================================
XI. READY-TO-PASTE MODULE TEXT
=====================================================================
Presumption applicable to everyone charged with a criminal offence

The European Convention on Human Rights applies the presumption of innocence. Article 6(2) of the Convention, in the text as amended through Protocol No. 15, provides:

  "Everyone charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law."

Source: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, opened for signature 4 November 1950, Rome, ETS No. 005, 213 U.N.T.S. 221 (entered into force 3 September 1953), as amended by Protocols Nos. 11 (ETS No. 155), 14 (CETS No. 194) and 15 (CETS No. 213), Article 6(2).

Note for learners: Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213, Strasbourg, 24 June 2013, in force 1 August 2021) amended the Convention's preamble and its Articles 21, 23, 30 and 35. It did not amend Article 6. The wording of Article 6(2) is unchanged since 1950.

=====================================================================
XII. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST BEFORE THE MODULE IS SIGNED OFF
=====================================================================

question: Y132
answer:
MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW. NOT LEGAL ADVICE.

JURISDICTION: United States federal administrative adjudication before the Federal Trade Commission under the Commission's Rules of Practice, 16 C.F.R. Part 3. The result below is jurisdiction-specific; Part 3 periods do not carry over to other agencies' adjudications or to Article III/state court practice.

QUESTION PRESENTED: In a single-respondent FTC adjudication governed by 16 C.F.R. Part 3 as in force on 2026-11-21, where the respondent uses the entire answer period and the ALJ then uses the entire period allowed after that answer to hold the scheduling conference, what is the combined interval from service of the complaint to the conference, using only those two stated periods?

SHORT ANSWER: 24 days (14 + 10), stated in calendar days.

I. GOVERNING TEXT (primary sources)

1. Answer period — 16 C.F.R. § 3.12(a) ("Time for filing"): "A respondent shall file an answer within 14 days after being served with the complaint." Source note appended in the Code of Federal Regulations: [74 FR 1820, Jan. 13, 2009]. Retrieved from the eCFR section view for 16 C.F.R. § 3.12 (title-16/part-3), capture dated 2026-11-23T10:55:28Z, sha256 04079c984ad8.

2. Scheduling conference — 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(b) ("Scheduling conference"): "Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference." Retrieved from the eCFR section view for 16 C.F.R. § 3.21, capture dated 2026-11-23T10:55:27Z, sha256 c96bee111904; identical text retrieved from the eCFR subpart C view, sha256 23587402d80c.

3. Corroborating Federal Register source: FTC, Rules of Practice (16 C.F.R. Parts 3 and 4), 74 Fed. Reg. 1820 (Jan. 13, 2009) — the amendment from which both current periods descend (the § 3.12 source note cites it; the January 13, 2009 rules document in the FTC's own repository states § 3.21(b) in the same 10-day form: "Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference," https://search.ftc.gov/sites/default/files/documents/federal_register_notices/rules-practice-16-cfr-parts-3-and-4/090113rulesofpractice.pdf, sha256 7b30f773e498).

4. Related provisions that do NOT add to the interval but are needed to read it correctly:
   - 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(a): counsel "shall meet" no later than 5 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, "[a]s early as practicable before the prehearing scheduling conference." This meeting falls inside the 10-day window and adds nothing.
   - 16 C.F.R. § 3.21(c)(1): the prehearing scheduling order is entered "[n]ot later than 2 days after the scheduling conference" — it falls after the conference and is outside the measured interval.
   - 16 C.F.R. § 3.11(b)(4): the complaint must give notice of the evidentiary hearing date (5 months from the administrative complaint where Section 13(b) relief is sought, 8 months otherwise). That date is fixed at the front end and is not part of the two stated periods.

II. CALCULATION

Step 1 — Service to answer. Service of the complaint starts the clock. Respondent uses the full 14 days under § 3.12(a) and files on the last permitted day. Cumulative: 14 days.

Step 2 — Answer to conference. The ALJ uses the full period under § 3.21(b) and holds the conference on the 10th day after the answer is filed. Cumulative: 14 + 10 = 24 days.

Step 3 — Single-respondent point. § 3.21(b) runs from the answer "filed by the last answering respondent." In a one-respondent proceeding the last (and only) answering respondent is that respondent, so no additional lag from co-respondents arises and the full 10 days is available in every case.

RESULT: 24 days from service of the complaint to the scheduling conference.

III. WHY THE "AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21" CONSTRAINT MATTERS (the numbers have moved)

These two figures are not stable across Part 3's history, which is why the operative-date constraint is load-bearing:
- 1996 amendments: § 3.12(a) answer at 14 days; § 3.21(b) conference within 7 calendar days after the answer (the accompanying statement of basis and purpose expressly says "within seven (7) calendar days after filing of the answer"). FTC, Rules of Practice Amendments (16 C.F.R. Parts 2, 3 and 4) (Sept. 26, 1996), https://www.ftc.gov/sites/default/files/documents/federal_register_notices/rules-practice-amendments-16-cfr-parts-2-3-and-4/960926rulesofpracticeamendments.pdf, sha256 6340de71c430. Combined: 21 days. (The Federal Register volume/page for this document was not verifiable from the retrieved pages and is deliberately not stated.)
- 2001/2003 rulemaking: § 3.12(a) proposed at "twenty (20) days after being served with the complaint" and § 3.21(b) at "fourteen (14) days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent." FTC, Rules of Practice (16 C.F.R. Parts 2, 3 and 4), https://search.ftc.gov/sites/default/files/documents/federal_register_notices/rules-practice-16-cfr-part-2-3-and-4/010403rulesofpractice.pdf, sha256 7fea3af0fba7. Combined: 34 days. (Federal Register citation not verifiable from the retrieved pages; not stated.)
- 2009 to date: 14 days (§ 3.12(a)) and 10 days (§ 3.21(b)), per the sources in Part I. Combined: 24 days.
A Part 3 amendment effective between the capture date and 2026-11-21 changing either figure is the only thing that would disturb the 24-day result; see the verification step in Part V.

IV. SCOPE OF THE ANSWER — WHAT IS AND IS NOT COUNTED

Per the request's instruction to use only the two stated periods, the following are excluded: any extension of the answer date by the ALJ; any tolling (e.g., the stay and tolling provisions attaching to a post-preliminary-injunction motion to dismiss, 16 C.F.R. § 3.22(d)(2)); any motion practice between answer and conference; the 5-day meet-and-confer under § 3.21(a) (subsumed inside the 10 days); and the 2-day scheduling order under § 3.21(c)(1) (after the conference). "Entire answer period" is read as the maximum period allowed with no waiver, no early filing, and no extension.

V. COMPUTATION CONVENTION — WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN, AND WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE

I did not retrieve a Part 3 general computation-of-time provision in the sources fetched, so I do not assert one. Two consequences, stated plainly:
(a) The sum of the two stated periods is 24 days regardless of convention. That is the answer to the question asked, and the request directs that only these two periods be used.
(b) If a Part 3 computation rule (or the practice of the Secretary/ALJ) excludes the trigger day and/or rolls a period ending on a weekend or federal holiday to the next business day, the actual calendar date of the conference could land on day 23, 24 or 25 counted from service. The memo therefore reports the interval as 24 days and flags a ±1-day calendar-date sensitivity; it does not assert a specific calendar date. This is the one point on which the authority located is thin, and it should be confirmed against the Part 3 text in force on the operative date before any date is calendared.

VI. VERIFICATION STEP BEFORE RELIANCE

The eCFR captures used are dated 2026-11-23T10:55Z — two days after the operative date of 2026-11-21. Before relying on the 24-day figure, confirm § 3.12(a) and § 3.21(b) against the eCFR point-in-time view for 2026-11-21 (or the corresponding annual CFR edition plus any Federal Register document effective on or before that date). If either figure differs in that snapshot, substitute it and re-add; the method above is unchanged.

VII. STATUS

This is a research draft for review by a qualified attorney. Every statement of law above is tied to the regulation text or Federal Register document cited; no statement of law is offered on any other jurisdiction.
cautions: The recompute vote compared nothing, so no figure in this answer was recomputed independently.

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 10 on ecfr.gov/current/title-16/part-3/section-3.21 and 7 on ftc.gov/sites/default/files/documents/federal_register_notices/rules-practice-amendments-16-cfr-parts-2-3-and-4/960926rulesofpracticeamendments.pdf. The first reads: "Not later than 10 days after the answer is filed by the last answering respondent, the Administrative Law Judge shall hold a scheduling conference."
The answer gives 24 calendar days for ask 5, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.
